In Au-Au collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 3 GeV, we investigate the formation of light nuclei, including deuterons, tritons, and helium-3, through the coalescence model, focusing on their production in different coalescence regions. Our findings indicate that the coalescence mechanism is effective in explaining the transverse momentum spectra of light nuclei, but struggles to reproduce their pT-integrated cross sections. We discover that the coalescence of nucleons from mini-jets in the central coalescence region is the primary source of light nuclei, while the coalescence of nucleons from corona and squeeze-out regions in the peripheral coalescence region contributes less significantly.

The discovery of thousands of exoplanets has led to a significant shift in the field of astrobiology, with the focus now being on understanding the habitability of various planetary systems. In this review, we will examine the current state of knowledge regarding the atmospheric and planetary science of exoplanetary systems, with a particular emphasis on rocky planets. We will explore the methods used to analyze the atmospheres of these planets, both directly and indirectly, and discuss the key findings in this area. The review will also cover the current state of modeling and simulation techniques, including photochemical modeling and radiative transfer, and discuss the role of future missions and advancements in technology. The review will conclude with a discussion of the future directions and challenges in the field of atmospheric science of exoplanetary systems.

A graph G is defined as dispersable if it can be mapped to a torus T_mn, n, m being positive integers, in such a way that every vertex of G is assigned a distinct set of coordinates. In this study, we establish criteria for the circulant graphs C_n(A) to be dispersable, where A represents a set of integers.

This work presents an enhanced family of accelerated iterative matrix inversion methods, capable of achieving faster convergence rates through the integration of multiple iterative techniques. The proposed methods are particularly well-suited for parallel and distributed processing environments and can be effectively utilized in scenarios involving matrix inversion. A key focus is placed on optimizing these methods for high-performance GPU computing. To this end, a comprehensive analysis of the proposed methods is provided, accompanied by a comparison against existing state-of-the-art approaches. A series of numerical experiments are conducted to validate the proposed methods' performance, with a special emphasis on their potential for GPU acceleration.

This paper delves into the power spectrum of primordial fluctuations in ultra-slow-roll inflation scenarios, incorporating the impact of non-Gaussianity through non-linear dynamics. Building on a previous study that introduced a non-linear modification to the slow-roll approximation, we apply this approach to a general potential, allowing for a broad range of ultra-slow-roll limits. We then derive the power spectrum of the perturbations using the slow-roll approximation and calculate the leading and sub-leading non-Gaussianity corrections, also providing numerical solutions to non-linear equations. Our findings indicate that non-Gaussianity has a significant effect on the power spectrum during ultra-slow-roll inflation, resulting in a suppression of power on large scales and an enhancement on smaller scales.

In a refined assortment problem, a decision-maker offers a curated selection of products tailored to individual customers' preferences, aiming to maximize profit while controlling offering costs. We introduce the refined assortment optimization problem and develop an algorithm to solve it efficiently. We also analyze the problem's performance under different cost constraints and establish bounds on the optimal solution. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of our approach to a broader customer segmentation problem.

In the field of survival analysis, researchers often rely on time-to-event data to understand how patients or objects recover from specific events or undergo treatment. Traditional methods typically model time-to-event distributions using parametric or non-parametric approaches, but these models can be flawed due to their sensitivity to incorrect assumptions. Moreover, the complexity of parametric models can hinder their application in real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, a new approach called the casebase method is proposed. This method involves estimating the duration of time until an event by calculating the average time until the last observed event for each group of interest. The estimated durations serve as indicators of the relative risks of future events within each group. The casebase method has been found to be more robust than conventional survival analysis techniques, making it a valuable tool for researchers.

Future high-precision experiments in physics necessitate the precise calculation of Feynman integrals across diverse kinematic scales. This calculation is complicated by the presence of scales in both the numerator and denominator, making it challenging to apply existing reduction techniques. In this study, we introduce a novel set of auxiliary dimensions to simplify the calculation of multi-scale Feynman integrals up to arbitrary loop orders. Our approach enables the creation of numerical programs to compute these integrals with high accuracy. As a proof of concept, we have developed a numerical program to compute a specific set of multi-scale Feynman integrals relevant to the Standard Model and its beyond, using a real-valued integration method that allows for efficient computation.

High-performance object stores are gaining traction as a viable alternative to traditional file systems, offering scalable data management for objects. This paper compares the performance of two systems, DAOS and Lustre, in a comprehensive benchmark, evaluating their capabilities for storing and processing object-based data. The experiments reveal that both systems excel in object storage, with Lustre showing superior performance in read operations and DAOS surpassing it in write operations and data access. DAOS outpaces Lustre in data transfer rates, achieving significantly higher bandwidth. The results demonstrate that both systems are well-suited for diverse applications, with Lustre more effectively handling read operations and DAOS excelling in data storage and transfer.

The increasing popularity of electric vehicles has led to the development of specialized parking facilities designed exclusively for EV users. However, these EV-only parking facilities often lack an efficient admission control system, resulting in long waiting times for vehicles seeking a parking spot. To address this issue, we propose an online admission control framework that optimizes parking lot utilization while minimizing waiting times. This system utilizes real-time data from a smart parking system, enabling a control unit to make informed decisions about accepting or rejecting vehicles. To evaluate its performance, we compare the proposed system with a baseline approach that prioritizes fairness and fairness-based policies. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving high acceptance rates, low waiting times, and efficient parking lot management.

We prove the existence of Euclidean and Hermitian linear complementary dual (LCD) codes with different parameters within finite fields. Additionally, we present methods for generating multiple Hermitian LCD codes and expanding Euclidean or Hermitian LCD codes with specific parameters within finite fields.

We show that classical general relativity can be obtained from loop amplitudes. 
By applying the principles of local supersymmetry, we establish a relationship between tree-level graviton scattering amplitudes and loop amplitudes involving massless fermions. 
This connection yields the correct low-energy predictions for gravitational interactions, including the gravitational wave polarization states. 
Notably, our approach provides a model-independent framework for understanding quantum gravity, and it does so without requiring the presence of matter fields in the theory.

The shift towards renewable energy sources, particularly solar and wind power, necessitates the expansion of land for these facilities, potentially encroaching on private and public lands. To gauge the impact of various decarbonization scenarios, we developed a model that balances land use changes and electricity generation, and applied it to the 12-state Western Electricity Coordinating Council region. The results indicate that decarbonization can be achieved without extensive land use transformations if certain strategies are adopted, such as prioritizing solar power and leveraging underutilized federal and private lands.

Cluster-randomized trials are frequently utilized for evaluating the impact of vaccines, yet developing suitable estimators and statistical methods to analyze these trials has proven to be a complex task. This challenge arises from the necessity to account for the inter-club correlations between participating groups. This review aims to provide an overview of various estimation approaches employed in cluster-randomized trials, including unbiased estimators, intention-to-treat, per-protocol, and as-treated methods. Additionally, we discuss statistical tests and confidence intervals used in conjunction with these estimators, and highlight specific considerations required for assessing the vaccine's efficacy in a cluster-randomized design.

This paper delves into the normalized Laplacian spectrum of the M-octagonal network, derived from the Sierpinski Gasket, and explores its connections to fractal M-octagonal networks. The research also extends to various characteristics of these networks, including connectivity, degree, energy, and energy difference, with further applications in detecting communities, graph comparison, and multi-dimensional scaling. The findings are supported by numerical examples that verify the proposed methods and their outcomes.

We introduce a contextual linear bandit algorithm capable of being implemented across a network structure, where a central node connects to various agents that each receive a unique subset of contextual variables. Unlike previous work, our algorithm allows for linear regret reduction with only shared mean reward estimates, not individual reward estimates or variables. The algorithm is based on a decentralized gradient descent method with a novel communication strategy, derived from the linear algebra of Kronecker products. We compare our algorithm to existing solutions and demonstrate its improved performance through theoretical results and numerical simulations.

The integration of data-driven approaches in healthcare has been increasingly prominent, with their adoption in clinical and research settings driven by the growing availability of large-scale, high-quality datasets. However, the effectiveness of these approaches relies heavily on the presence of such datasets. Consequently, the development of synthetic data has become a crucial area of research, as it enables the creation of realistic data sets that can be used in place of their real-world counterparts. This research focuses on synthesizing electronic health records for patients with cystic fibrosis, utilizing a combination of recurrent neural networks and medical domain knowledge to generate accurate data sets. The proposed approach is evaluated using a range of performance metrics, as well as a medical expert review of the synthesized data.

Decays of the $D^{0}$ meson into specific combinations of hadrons are analyzed using a dataset collected by the LHCb experiment. The dataset consists of 3 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data. The analysis focuses on two main decay modes, $D^{0} \to K^{0}SK^{*}(892)^{0}$ and $D^{0} \to K^{0}SK^{*}(800)^{0}$, and their respective isobar models. The study provides precise measurements of the $K^{*}(892)^{0}$ mass and width, as well as the branching fraction of the $D^{0} \to K^{0}SK^{+}K^{-}$ decay relative to the $D^{0} \to K^{0}SK^{0}K^{0}$ decay. The analysis also investigates the properties of the $K^{*}(800)^{0}$ meson and the $D^{0} \to K^{0}SK^{0}K^{0}$ decay amplitude.

Novelpy (v1.2) is an open-source Python package that calculates novelty and disruptiveness metrics for bibliometric and patent data, including citations, news, and related references, providing diverse calculation methods and data visualization tools. This package's calculations are based on established methods from literature reviews, and it offers flexibility through custom functions and a clear API for easy extension and adaptation. Novelpy is available under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and can be installed from the Python Package Index.

We've developed a method to precisely control the beam profile of lasers using cross-phase modulation with laser pulses. Our technique enables the creation of complex, user-controllable intensity patterns in the target area by adjusting the transverse intensity of the driving pulse. We demonstrate this capability by generating specific shapes such as a '7' and a swan-like pattern, as well as controlling the shape of a Gaussian beam. This technique offers potential applications in laser-based manufacturing, such as cutting and drilling, where it can be used to create customized intensity patterns in a short period of time.

Humanoid robotics has advanced significantly, allowing robots to perform various tasks similar to humans in multiple environments. However, humanoid robots struggle with tasks requiring precision and dexterity, such as shooting a bow and arrow. We investigate the feasibility of a humanoid robot performing this task, and to assess our research progress, we have established a robotic system for shooting a recurve bow at the University of California, Santa Cruz. We have also created a simulation model to predict the trajectory of a recurve arrow and the robot's shooting process.

The growing diversity in user preferences and the increasing number of available items pose significant challenges to the field of recommendation systems. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring cross-domain recommendation (CDR) methods that utilize data from multiple domains to improve recommendation accuracy. However, existing CDR techniques often struggle with scalability due to the diverse and complex nature of available data. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach called Dual Metric Learning (DML), which aims to enhance the performance of CDR methods by learning dual metrics from user preferences and item similarities. By leveraging a novel metric learning method, DML enables the efficient and effective utilization of data, regardless of its complexity or source. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DML in improving various CDR methods, while also showcasing its ability to adapt to different scenarios, domains, and item types.

We propose a characterization for the modal $\mu$-calculus within a specific framework of distributed automata, where the local automata do not need to be connected in a network and can process modal operators asynchronously, leading to a more efficient and fair distributed model. This characterization is based on a type of bisimulation equivalence, where the local automata are compared to the global modal $\mu$-calculus, and involves a new definition of distributed fixed points, where the local automata are able to make independent decisions about the order of evaluation. This characterization also leads to a new decidability result for a specific fragment of the modal $\mu$-calculus, where the local automata are restricted in their use of the next-time operator.

The thermal conductivity of a 2D system can be accurately measured by analyzing heat waves that propagate through it. This study focuses on a 2D plasma system within a specific setup, the Rotating Dust Yttrium Plasma Experiment. It was discovered that the thermal conductivity in this system increases linearly with its conductivity, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the unique properties of 2D thermal transport. This system's properties can be further enhanced by adjusting the rotation speed, thereby increasing its thermal conductivity. This study provides valuable insights into the thermal transport properties of 2D plasma systems, an area of research that is crucial for understanding heat transfer in various environments.

We examine linear combinations of unsorted lists of numerical values, 
considering both exact and approximate calculations, and how rounding affects the outcome. 
The objective is to determine the linear combination that most closely approximates a target value 
while minimizing the maximum discrepancy among the vector components. 
This problem is equivalent to minimizing the maximum absolute error and is a classic problem 
in the field of computer science and operations research, with applications in computer 
vision, machine learning, and data analysis.

Cardiac angiography, a critical diagnostic tool, utilizes X-ray radiation to capture images of blood vessels, but frequent image taking increases the risk of radiation damage to living cells. Our research demonstrates that by employing a deep convolutional neural network, we can effectively reconstruct and improve image quality using video interpolation, thereby reducing the need for repeated X-ray exposures by up to 50%.

The study of heavy-flavour quarks will be a key area of research at the FCC-ee, an electron-positron collider that will provide unparalleled precision in many areas. This precision is due to the machine's exceptional $e^+e^-$ collision properties, which include high luminosity, extremely low background interference, and a mass range spanning from 60 GeV to 100 GeV. This will enable researchers to explore a vast territory of heavy-flavour physics, from the study of bottom and charm quarks to the investigation of exotic particles. This article will outline the main research objectives for heavy-flavour physics at FCC-ee, focusing on the production of certain types of particles and the decay processes of b-hadrons.

The interaction between dark matter and a specific type of particle has been found to be limited by a neutrino-related constraint. In models involving a new force of nature, particle interactions are restricted by a specific threshold when the rate of dark matter annihilation is influenced by the presence of electrons. This paper examines the implications of this constraint on a specific type of model, in which the interaction between dark matter and a lepton subsector is unique. By analyzing the model's parameters, we investigate the impact of this constraint on a specific type of particle interaction and compare the results with existing limits on a related particle interaction.

The formation of binary systems with massive stars can result in the ejection of hypervelocity stars (HVSs) from the Galactic Center, potentially influencing the observed population of HVSs. We investigated the long-term evolution of binary systems with a massive companion star using a new method. Our results show that the binary system's eccentricity increases over time due to the massive companion's perturbation, leading to the separation of the companion from the primary star. This separation can result in the ejection of the primary star as an HVS, with a significant fraction of the binary systems experiencing this outcome. The orbital distribution of the ejective binary systems is influenced by the pre-ejection eccentricity, with a higher eccentricity corresponding to a more eccentric ejection direction. Our results also indicate that the ejective binary systems have a higher probability of being detected as HVSs due to their higher velocities and a longer detection distance. The observed HVSs from the Galactic Center are likely to have ejective binary systems with a pre-ejection eccentricity of 0.8-0.9.

This paper explores a specific category of multiplicative stochastic differential equations. By establishing connections to related fields such as probability, physics and finance, we obtain new insights into weak solutions. Our primary contribution lies in applying a novel approach to derive existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for these equations. This approach differs from traditional methods like Pettis integration and Girsanov's formula, and instead leverages the relationship between these equations and a class of stochastic differential equations with noise perturbation, known as stochastic gradient systems.

We examine the implications of the Forcing Axiom $P(\omega_1)$ and its variants, $PFA$ and $PFA^{++}$, on the properties of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$. Specifically, we investigate whether these axioms enable the creation of nonstationary ideals with specific properties through $\omega_1$-sequence forcing, and conclude that neither $PFA$ nor $PFA^{++}$ facilitate this. However, we show that the combination of $P(\omega_1)$ and an additional axiom, namely $\omega_1$:: \omega_1, is sufficient to realize such ideals.

Pre-trained language models have been successfully adapted to various downstream tasks, yet their adaptation process remains largely opaque and inflexible. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework called Adaptor, which enables a more objective-driven and modular adaptation approach. Adaptor treats the adaptation process as a collection of objectives, each of which can be adapted independently to produce a specific function. To achieve this, we propose a novel method that allows for the creation of a universal Adaptor by learning a set of parameterized functions. We demonstrate that Adaptor can be effectively trained using a combination of objectives, and show that it outperforms existing methods on a range of tasks, including text classification and language modeling. Additionally, we show that Adaptor's modular design facilitates the creation of a compact and efficient adaptation framework that achieves state-of-the-art performance on a set of text classification tasks.

A comprehensive dataset of 13,500 annotated traffic signs from around the world, captured by vehicles in 12 countries, is presented to facilitate the development of global traffic sign detection and classification systems. The dataset's diverse distribution, achieved through a structured collection process, ensures that it accurately represents a wide range of traffic sign types, shapes, and colors found in different countries. The dataset's effectiveness for traffic sign detection and classification is demonstrated, particularly in comparison to datasets focused on Western countries, and is shown to be valuable for applications requiring a diverse set of traffic signs worldwide.

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning have led to promising outcomes in various domains, including computer vision and natural language processing. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by exploring self-supervised learning in the context of collaborative filtering for recommendation systems. To achieve this, we introduce a novel framework, SelfCF, which leverages diverse visual and textual data associated with user-item interactions to derive meaningful representations. Through a comprehensive evaluation on real-world datasets, our proposed framework SelfCF surpasses the performance of existing state-of-the-art methods, including both supervised and self-supervised approaches.
We provide a complete classification of the TEvelev degrees of projective spaces of any dimension, using a modified approach inspired by the TEvelev degree concept for curves.

A novel gapped Dirac semimetal is proposed, featuring linear and parabolic dispersions in the same phase. This phase is characterized by a unique structure, consisting of a parabolic Dirac point in the bulk, surrounded by linear dispersion zones in the surface states. By applying an external magnetic field, the linear and parabolic regions can be separated, resulting in a zero-energy mode emerging at the Dirac point. Our findings suggest that this gapped Dirac semimetal offers a viable platform for creating a topological insulator with mixed linear and parabolic dispersions.

We examine the local model of a slow and stable meromorphic curve as it exits a main component of the extended phase space and enters a nearby one under the action of a group, analogous to the Jacobian group. We demonstrate that the sequence of points where the curve enters and exits the extended phase space exhibits the "good" properties of a "good" sequence in the sense of S. Bolotov, thereby enabling the application of the "good" sequence theorem to determine the Jacobian group's rank.

Future third-generation ground-based detectors will have the capability to observe gravitational waves from compact binary mergers at distances of hundreds of Mpc. This study focuses on the detection prospects of gravitational wave higher-order modes, which contain key information about the source and the detector itself. We examine the detection of these modes in various signals, including inspiraling binaries, and identify specific conditions necessary for their detection. We also analyze the constraints on detector parameters and the potential for measuring mode amplitudes, which could reveal new information about future detectors.

Astronomers have long been fascinated by the possibility of observing compact objects, such as black holes or neutron stars, in binary systems. By utilizing astrometric methods, researchers can detect these celestial bodies even if they don't emit their own light. In this study, we employ Gaia's astrometry to identify 13 binary systems containing a compact object, which has been previously discovered by the LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA Collaboration. Our analysis focuses on using Gaia's astrometric data to measure the binary's orbital path, which allows us to determine the mass of the compact object. Our results show that the masses of the compact objects in these binary systems are consistent with those of black holes, with estimated masses ranging from 14 to 70 solar masses.

This research paper delves into the convergence of the genetic algorithm in solving 0/1 knapsack problems, focusing on the influence of various selection methods and crossover techniques. The study evaluates the performance of genetic algorithms paired with rank selection, tournament selection, and uniform selection, alongside uniform, cycle, and compound crossover methods. The findings are based on the computational results of 15 benchmark problems from the commonly used instances in the literature. The results indicate that a combination of tournament selection and cycle crossover yields the highest convergence rate, outperforming other permutations of these operators. Additionally, a novel compound crossover technique is proposed, which integrates cycle and composition crossovers, and is shown to enhance the convergence of the genetic algorithm when paired with tournament selection.

This paper examines oscillatory integrals with three distinct convolutions in two-dimensional space, deriving decay rates for their Fourier transforms and estimating Lebesgue spaces norms for their derivatives.

The application of large language models to hate speech detection has been hindered by the lack of extensive, publicly accessible datasets. To bridge this gap, we have created a large, annotated dataset of hate speech and developed a method for generating additional labeled data using the T5 model. This approach involves fine-tuning the T5 model on hate speech data and then leveraging it to label new texts, which are then incorporated into the original dataset. Our results demonstrate that this expanded dataset leads to significant improvements in hate speech detection when used in conjunction with the T5 model. Furthermore, we have established a new state-of-the-art performance on the HateXplain dataset by combining the T5 model with a BERT-based classifier, achieving an F1 score of 0.94.

We examine the computational requirements for quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods in the context of ions with complex electronic structures. Our analysis focuses on the impact of ion charge and the computational resources needed to achieve a specific level of accuracy in forces. We investigate the feasibility of using a single, systematically designed basis set for a range of ions with different charge states. Our results demonstrate that the computational cost of QMC forces increases with ion charge to a power of 2.5 to 3.0. However, we also find that the accuracy of forces improves with ion charge to a power of 1.5 to 2.0. To mitigate the increased computational cost associated with higher-charge ions, we propose a strategy for combining QMC and density functional theory calculations. Our approach involves using DFT to determine the electronic structure of the most complex ion and then using QMC to determine the electronic structure of the remaining ions. Our numerical simulations demonstrate the feasibility of this strategy, showing that the computational cost of this approach is significantly reduced, particularly for ions with high charges.

The 2020 US presidential election was marred by allegations of widespread voter fraud, which social media platforms were a primary source for. Despite the significant impact of these claims, there is a lack of research on their content and spread. To address this knowledge gap, we created the VoterFraud2020 dataset, a comprehensive collection of election-related misinformation on Twitter. The dataset includes 1.7 million tweets from 700 accounts that made over 3.5 million claims across 13 categories of alleged election misconduct. Additionally, we developed a method to identify and remove bot accounts, resulting in a dataset of 1.3 million human-operated accounts that made 2.9 million fraudulent claims. The dataset's analysis reveals that most claims were made by a small group of partisans, and that these claims were often shared through retweets and replies. Furthermore, we found that these claims were frequently accompanied by misinformation, and that this misinformation was often spread through echo chambers. The dataset's multi-modal nature also allows for the application of various multimodal methods, including the analysis of images and videos. The dataset's analysis has significant implications for the 2024 US election, highlighting the need for social media platforms to implement more effective measures to combat election misinformation.

We consider a C^2 diffeomorphism, f, with some positive Lyapunov exponent and one positive and at most two ergodic invariant measures, μ, with μ(S) > 0, where S is a stable set. Under the condition that two conditions are met: the Hausdorff dimension of μ almost everywhere is less than the dimension of M, and the Hausdorff dimension of S is greater than the product of the sum of the positive Lyapunov exponent and one and the Hausdorff dimension of μ almost everywhere, we establish that there exists a locally maximal invariant set, A, which satisfies that the Hausdorff dimension of μ almost everywhere is less than the dimension of A, and for any ergodic measure, ν, on A, its growth rate is greater than the positive Lyapunov exponent of f.

In Bayesian Neural Networks, predictive uncertainty is often quantified by approximating the posterior probability distribution using a Gaussian distribution, typically derived from the last layer's latent space. A common approach involves sampling the latent space and making predictions under the assumed distribution, or approximating the predictive distribution with Monte Carlo estimates based on these samples. However, this approach can be inadequate for certain tasks, particularly when the posterior distribution exhibits non-Gaussian behavior. In such cases, a more comprehensive strategy is to leverage the entire posterior distribution, rather than just a single sample or approximation. This study presents a novel approach, referred to as ENAP (ENcoding the ANterior APproxiimation), which utilizes a more accurate representation of the posterior distribution by encoding the anterior approximation's parameters. This enables the creation of more accurate predictive distributions, and is demonstrated to be effective in various scenarios, including regression, classification, and uncertainty calibration.

A widely recognized model for electron transfer, the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory, is often used to interpret experimental results. This model describes electron transfer between two metal sites through a vibrational bath, with a specific energy distribution that follows a Lorentz distribution. This model is typically used to analyze cases where the energy difference between the initial and final states is zero. However, we have developed a new approach to the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory that can be applied to cases where the energy difference is non-zero. This new approach is based on a quantum mechanical model of electron transfer, with a specific Hamiltonian that includes a vibrational bath. This model is then reduced to a simpler, more manageable form using a semiclassical approximation. This approximation allows us to calculate the rate of electron transfer, with a specific energy distribution that is consistent with the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory. This new approach is an extension of the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory, with a specific energy distribution that is consistent with the Lorentz distribution. This new approach is also applicable to cases where the energy difference between the initial and final states is non-zero.

This research introduces a novel control design method, combining elements of Model Predictive Control and optimal control theories. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, the proposed strategy achieves efficient and safe operation. To demonstrate its effectiveness, a case study involving a cooperative vehicle system is presented, where multiple vehicles must navigate to a common target while navigating through a cluttered environment with static obstacles. The study showcases the performance of the proposed method under different scenarios, including those with limited visibility and the presence of slower-moving vehicles.

A theoretical model is developed to explain the thermoelectric effect in a thin film of a Heusler alloy, specifically the half-Heusler $TtX$ compound with $Tt$ being NiPd or NiPt and $X$ being P or As. This model incorporates the band structure and transport properties of both conduction electrons in the conduction band and the thermal motion of magnons in the spin-waves system. It is found that the thermopower and Seebeck coefficient of this system can be described by the equation $\frac{\pi}{4}k_B$ times the logarithm of the ratio between the spin-waves energy and the band energy. This results in a potential for a significant thermoelectric effect in thin films of $Tt$As due to the large difference between the magnon energy and the band energy.

The Perfect Sum problem, a classic combinatorial challenge, demands identifying whether integer $N$ can be expressed as the sum of $k$ distinct positive integers. $N$ is represented as the sum of $k$ numbers $x_i$, where each $x_i$ is an integer greater than or equal to 1. This work introduces a novel probabilistic method to confirm the solvability of Perfect Sum for any given $N$ and $k$. The proposed method is also adaptable for determining the existence of $n$ distinct integers forming a perfect sum, and it can be applied to both positive and negative integers. Additionally, this approach has been implemented in Python and can be accessed through the GitHub repository https://github.com/ArtemSlvt/combinatorial-problems.

Let q be an odd prime power, with F_q denoting the corresponding finite field. This paper focuses on the finite field F_q[x]/<f> where f is a polynomial of the form x^m+a, with m being at most (q-1)/2 and a a non-zero element in F_q. The study centers around the probability that randomly chosen elements in this field are of an order equal to or greater than m, providing an asymptotic formula for this probability when both m and q tend to infinity in a way that m/q remains finite.

This study outlines the findings from an investigation into automated source code analysis, specifically focusing on its connection to model checking, a technique for verifying a system's behavior against a predefined specification. The research demonstrates the practical application of UPPAAL, a well-known model checking tool, in this context, showcasing its capabilities and limitations when applied to model-based program analysis.

Recent advancements in metasurfaces have led to the development of innovative imaging systems capable of capturing detailed information about the environment around them. By utilizing these systems, researchers can create various imaging techniques, such as diffraction-limited imaging, that leverage the unique properties of metasurfaces to produce high-quality images. However, the implementation of these systems is often hindered by the limitations of available materials, which can restrict their performance. To overcome these challenges, researchers have proposed a novel approach that leverages artificial intelligence and signal processing to optimize metasurfaces for specific tasks, such as compressive sensing. By using a genetic algorithm to optimize the design of metasurfaces, researchers can significantly improve the quality of images, which can then be reconstructed using advanced signal processing algorithms. This research demonstrates the potential of artificial intelligence and signal processing to push the boundaries of metasurfaces and create innovative imaging technologies.

We have observed distinct signatures of high-order harmonics in an intense laser field with a specific circular polarization and frequency structure. The creation of these high-order harmonics is influenced by a specific interaction between the laser field components and specific atomic properties. The resulting spectral patterns are characterized by a specific symmetry and frequency arrangement. The observed patterns show a specific relationship with the laser field components and harmonic order, and are affected by a specific energy shift caused by the laser field. The observed patterns are consistent with theoretical predictions and have the potential to be used in an experimental measurement of a specific laser field property.

Image blending techniques have been developed to combine two images, but these methods typically rely on either a pre-defined mask or manual editing to achieve a seamless result. However, manually creating a mask can be time-consuming and requires skilled image processing. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called SemanticMix, which automatically generates a mask for blending two images without requiring manual intervention. By leveraging a semantic segmentation model, SemanticMix can automatically create a mask for combining two images, resulting in a more realistic and seamless result. To further enhance the quality of the blended image, we also propose a loss function that encourages the blended image to resemble the original images, rather than just a weighted average of the two images. Experimental results demonstrate that SemanticMix outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in image blending.

The expression of genes in living organisms is a complex process influenced by the interactions of various factors, resulting in wide variability in the production of mRNA and proteins. Although this noise might seem detrimental to the functioning of living systems, it has been found to play a crucial role in the adaptation and survival of living systems. The study of gene expression noise has been an area of focus in recent years, with researchers seeking to understand its mechanisms and effects on the functioning of living systems. In this study, we aim to develop a theoretical framework for analyzing stochastic trajectories of gene expression, with a focus on extracting meaningful information from these trajectories. The analysis of gene expression trajectories involves the identification of the optimal time for measurement, as well as the determination of the necessary sample size and measurement precision required to extract meaningful information from these trajectories. The proposed framework is based on the concept of information gain, with a focus on the information gain associated with the mean expression level of genes. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this framework by applying it to a simple model of gene expression, with a focus on the information gain associated with the mean expression level of genes. The study also discusses the potential applications of this framework in the analysis of gene expression noise in living systems.

In this research, we've developed a semi-supervised learning method that uses data analysis to determine the impact of each unlabeled example in a dataset. This data-driven approach relies on a model that identifies how these examples influence the labeled data, and then uses this information to optimize the model, resulting in improved performance on the labeled data. We've tested this method using different types of datasets and neural networks, and the findings show that the proposed algorithm can outperform traditional semi-supervised learning methods and in some cases the conventional supervised approach.

A widely used heuristic method called the Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) is employed to find solutions to complex optimisation problems. When the problem size is large, it's challenging to determine the optimal QAOA parameters. Our study reveals that for certain problems, it's possible to achieve optimal results with a limited number of layer QAOA parameters, suggesting a saturation point where further layers don't significantly improve the solution quality. Our findings are supported by theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, particularly in the context of the MaxCut problem.

Person re-identification is a complex task that aims to identify individuals across different images. This problem has garnered significant attention in recent years, prompting numerous studies. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the state-of-the-art approaches to re-identifying individuals across multiple camera views in various environments. Initially, we examine the underlying challenges of this issue, including the lack of distinct features and the sensitivity of the feature representation to camera angles and lighting conditions. Next, we delve into the fundamental techniques employed to address these challenges, including data enhancement, feature learning, and loss function optimization. Subsequently, we explore the recent advancements in the field, focusing on the use of advanced neural networks, such as siamese and triplet networks, and the incorporation of data augmentation and pre-training strategies. Finally, we conclude by highlighting promising research directions and outlining potential future research avenues.

The increasing availability of modern power system time series data has enabled researchers to tackle complex problems with greater ease, yet the data is often restricted to a single power system and not readily accessible for research purposes. This limitation has been addressed by developing a data-driven approach that utilizes publicly available time series data to reconstruct power system dynamics. This approach allows for the generation of power system time series with varying lengths and resolutions, and can be applied to multiple power systems. The effectiveness of the method has been demonstrated through its application to power systems from the United States and Australia, and has been used to generate power system load time series that exhibit various characteristics, including weather-sensitive load with high spatial and temporal resolution. This approach has the potential to support a wide range of power system research and development projects.

This study examines the convergence properties of a perturbed algorithm for solving a specific type of variational inequality problem. Our analysis demonstrates that under certain conditions, particularly strong monotonicity and the presence of a Lipschitzian perturbation, the algorithm's sequence of iterations converges strongly to the problem's unique solution.

We investigate the intersection points of closed geodesics within hyperbolic 2- and 3-dimensional geometry, and present a comprehensive classification of Fuchsian groups featuring a single 2-dimensional geodesic with an intersection point of two. Furthermore, we explore the Fuchsian groups generated by reflections across geodesics within hyperbolic 3-dimensional geometry, and establish a comprehensive classification of such groups based on the intersection patterns of their fundamental 2-dimensional geodesics.

A search for electron and muon pair decays from the $\Upsilon(3S)$ state is conducted using $1.02\times10^8$ $\Upsilon(3S)$ events obtained from data recorded with the BESIII detector at the BEPCII storage ring. No significant signal is detected, and the findings set stringent lower limits on the branching fraction ratio for the $\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\mp}$ decay relative to the $\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow \pi^0\gamma$ channel. These limits range from $1.4\times10^{-6}$ to $2.1\times10^{-6}$ at a 90% confidence level.

We investigated the effect of pressure on the flat-band Kagome compounds Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ with $x$ = 0, 0.25, and 0.50, measuring electrical resistivity and superconducting properties under various conditions. The compounds exhibit a superconducting transition at 3.8 K, 3.0 K, and 2.5 K respectively, with a transition width of approximately 0.1 K. Applying pressure resulted in a superconducting transition temperature increase of 0.5 K, 0.8 K, and 1.0 K respectively, with a corresponding enhancement in upper critical field. The superconducting transition temperature increases with increasing selenium content. The compounds exhibit a high superconducting transition width, suggesting a uniform superconducting transition. The superconducting transition temperature increase under pressure is consistent with a previously studied Kagome compound, suggesting a similar mechanism for the superconductivity in these flat-band compounds.

We investigate the recovery of information from black holes in three-dimensional JT gravity by analyzing the asymptotic symmetry algebra's operator product. We derive the operator product expansions for the asymptotic symmetry algebra of the BTZ black hole and the extremal wormhole using a covariant phase space approach, which allows us to relate the coefficients to the quasinormal modes or the geodesic motion. We then demonstrate that the information encoded in the Witten diagram corresponding to a BTZ black hole can be recovered by summing the information from its asymptotic symplectic Killing characteristics, with the process being analogous to the KdV soliton for the extremal wormhole.

Recent advancements in neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) have led to increased adoption in various fields. However, the influence of measurement inaccuracies on neural ODE (N-ODE) models has not been thoroughly investigated. To address this knowledge gap, we introduce a comprehensive framework for assessing the impact of measurement noise on neural ODE models. Our framework is based on a novel formulation of neural ODEs that enables the derivation of error bounds for these models. Notably, our formulation is independent of the specific neural network architecture used. Our experiments demonstrate that neural ODE models are highly susceptible to measurement noise, even when the data is close to the true trajectory. Furthermore, we develop a method for inferring the trajectory from noisy data and show that it can be interpreted as a form of trajectory smoothing. Our framework is versatile and can be applied to neural ODE models with both deterministic and stochastic differential equations.

We introduce a novel navigation method, the Object Memory Transformer, capable of learning from visual data in a simulated environment. The model incorporates a memory component that stores and retrieves visual information to reach specific objectives. By utilizing an object-based approach, the model learns to navigate to a target object, whereas traditional reinforcement learning methods often rely on arbitrary rewards. The model features an attention mechanism that enables it to retrieve and combine information from multiple camera views, facilitating the identification of the target objective. Our model demonstrates superior performance in goal-oriented navigation tasks, including object retrieval, compared to other navigation techniques.

The OPT-IML framework is a novel instruction meta-learning method, which utilizes a large language model to identify task-specific knowledge within its own knowledge graph. By incorporating a task-specific prompt generator and a task-specific generator, OPT-IML enables the model to generate task-specific text based on input instructions. Unlike previous approaches, which require pre-existing datasets, OPT-IML allows for generating task-specific text based on input instructions, facilitating the generation of new task data. Our evaluation of OPT-IML on GLUE and SuperGLUE datasets demonstrates that it outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, our analysis reveals that OPT-IML generalizes well to unseen tasks, which is a critical capability for real-world applications.

The primary goal of this research is to gain a deeper understanding of how novice users interact with the Scratch platform, specifically how they participate in various ways and what types of support they need to become more skilled. To achieve this goal, we analyzed a large dataset of user interactions and identified distinct types of user behavior, including different levels of participation and patterns associated with specific age groups and skill levels. Our findings suggest that users with similar age or skill levels exhibit similar patterns of participation, while users with different age or skill levels exhibit distinct patterns. Furthermore, our research reveals that users with different levels of experience exhibit different types of participation, suggesting that users require tailored support based on their individual needs and skill levels.

A novel approach to calculating electron correlation in a uniform electron gas is presented, utilizing a transcorrelated Hamiltonian and a host of correlated basis functions. This allows for a more accurate and efficient description of electrons at all wavelengths, particularly in the low electron gas density limit. By incorporating a perturbation theory, we can obtain correlation energies with high precision, and we have demonstrated the efficacy of this method by comparing our results to established benchmarks. Our findings show that the transcorrelation method can effectively capture the system's behavior across a wide range of densities, and provides a more accurate representation of the system's properties than traditional methods, particularly at lower densities.

We introduce a novel family of probability distributions that address uncertainty in location, taking into account both deterministic and random location shifts. These distributions are constructed by applying optimal transportation principles to a random space, where the density function is considered a random variable. The resulting distribution family includes a well-known probability measure, which is obtained when the density function is constant. The proposed distribution family is characterized by physical constraints that ensure its validity, and it can be used to model uncertainty in various real-world applications. Furthermore, this distribution family can be used to estimate error covariance in data assimilation and to represent uncertainty in ensemble data.

The advent of big data has led to a significant surge in data-driven applications, 
yet, ensuring data privacy and security in such systems poses a considerable 
challenge. This study introduces an innovative approach to safeguarding data
privacy by leveraging randomized tensor network decomposition and dispersed 
computation. The proposed method randomizes data distribution across multiple 
parties and employs tensor decomposition to transform data into a lower-rank 
representation. This technique is particularly effective in reducing high-dimensional 
data to a lower dimension, thereby enhancing privacy and security. Furthermore, 
it utilizes dispersed computation to distribute calculation responsibilities among 
multiple parties, thereby improving efficiency and scalability. The approach 
is also adaptable to various data formats, including structured and unstructured 
data. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this method in protecting data 
privacy and security, particularly in scenarios involving high-dimensional data.

In this study, we address the challenge of safely transferring learning-based control systems to real-world robots. We present SafeAPT, a straightforward yet effective method that leverages multiple policies simulated in diverse environments to ensure safe transfer. By utilizing a collection of policies trained on distinct simulation settings, we can generate a set of risk-averse trajectories that can be combined to form a safe path for the robot. This approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the robot interacts with dynamic, unpredictable environments. We evaluate SafeAPT in two tasks: navigating a dynamic indoor environment and a robotic arm scenario. Our results demonstrate that SafeAPT can successfully guarantee safety in 100% of cases, whereas existing methods fall short in this regard.

Radio galaxies and quasars are powerful astrophysical events that result from supermassive black holes. These events are characterized by the presence of energetic jets that emit radio signals. Observations of these jets have been conducted for decades, providing valuable insights into their behavior and properties. In this review, we discuss the current understanding of jet physics, focusing on the characteristics of radio galaxies and quasars. The radio universe is dominated by radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGN), with radio galaxies and quasars being their primary types. These objects are often classified based on their radio-loudness, with some galaxies and quasars emitting weak radio signals. The high-redshift radio quasars are thought to be among the most luminous objects in the universe, with some quasars detected at z > 6. Radio galaxies and quasars are often associated with powerful jets that emit synchrotron radiation, with some galaxies hosting multiple jets. The orientation of these jets relative to the sky plane is also an important factor, with some being viewed end-on and others as a side-on perspective. The study of jet physics is complex and challenging, with the understanding of jet acceleration and the role of magnetic fields still being unresolved. The presence of jet cavities and the interaction between the jet and its surroundings are also crucial factors in the evolution of these systems. The study of radio galaxies and quasars has the potential to provide insights into jet physics, the role of

This research focuses on a time-varying nonlinear regression model with time-invariant parameters and time-inhomogeneous innovations. We examine the asymptotic properties of the least squares estimators in a linear context and the quasi-maximum likelihood estimators in a nonlinear setting under mild conditions. Furthermore, we develop a simultaneous inference procedure for these estimators, which is essential for constructing confidence intervals and tests for parameter subspaces. The proposed method is validated through Monte Carlo simulations and applied to analyze the impact of climate change and global warming using historical data.

The widespread use of the internet has led to an increase in data, with a substantial portion of it consisting of information that is objectionable or unsuitable. This paper explores the development of techniques for identifying objectionable content, specifically text, which is a pressing concern due to its potential to cause harm. We examine the effectiveness of cutting-edge approaches for detecting objectionable language in both English and Turkish, utilizing sophisticated neural network models. Our research reveals that deep learning methods excel in this area, and we contribute to the field by presenting the most successful models and benchmarks for offense detection in English and Turkish.

The brain's functional connectivity, a network of interactions, is a key focus in neuroscience research.  Traditional methods for studying this topic rely heavily on preconceived ideas and specific tasks.  In contrast, our study uses a data-driven approach that doesn't require prior assumptions.  This new method leverages a deep learning technique to uncover patterns in brain activity and their functional relationships.  This approach was applied to resting state fMRI data from both healthy individuals and those with schizophrenia, revealing distinct patterns in brain connectivity.  Our findings not only offer fresh insights into the neural mechanisms behind schizophrenia but also demonstrate the potential for data-driven discovery in the field of neuroscience.

This research develops a comprehensive framework for assessing the efficiency of Nesterov's accelerated algorithm in solving convex optimization problems. The novel framework relies on a time-varying system model, incorporating a controlled element and interaction with the algorithmic process. The framework is grounded in dissipativity theory, a fundamental principle for analyzing control systems. The derived conditions for algorithmic efficiency are expressed in terms of the algorithm's parameters and the objective function's characteristics, providing a clear and straightforward interpretation. The study also offers a method for estimating the algorithm's performance based on its initial state and the system's transient dynamics. The research is supplemented by numerical experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

This research introduces a boundary handling strategy for implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods designed for hyperbolic systems with supplementary source terms, which maintains optimal positivity and efficient computational capabilities. The proposed approach leverages the high-order upwind method to approximate boundary conditions, enabling the use of explicit-implicit Runge-Kutta methods, which are suitable for approximating stiff hyperbolic systems. The resulting upwind-implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta method is capable of achieving optimal accuracy and maintaining positivity without requiring additional memory or operations. The proposed strategy is applied to the Burgers equation and the one-dimensional Euler equations, with numerical results demonstrating the method's effectiveness.

The thickness of photovoltaic and solar thermal conversion layers is often limited
by the need for optimal light absorption, but this constraint is alleviated by
back reflectors that enhance absorption in thin and ultrathin films, allowing
for more efficient light harnessing in these thin layers. Our study focuses on
the impact of back reflectors on light absorption rates in thin silicon films,
with particular emphasis on films of 20nm and 100nm thickness. Our results show
that a 3D photonic band gap reflector can boost absorption levels by up to 40%
in 20nm-thick films and 13% in 100nm-thin films, with the benefit persisting
even in scenarios where light is scattered.

This paper introduces Credal Valuation Networks, a novel graphical model that integrates credal sets into valuation networks. By modeling uncertainty within credal sets, Credal Valuation Networks enable the propagation of this uncertainty through network edges, generating a product set. We demonstrate how to efficiently compute the meet and join operations for Credal Valuation Networks within polynomial time, and we showcase an application in a Bayesian network for reasoning under uncertainty conditions. Furthermore, we discuss the implementation of Credal Valuation Networks in the open-source software RAVEN.

Top-K recommendation systems often rely on a distance metric learning framework, 
which typically involves incorporating a margin term to ensure the distance 
between recommended and non-recommended items is substantial, with the recommended 
item distance being minimal. However, the margin term's fixed structure limits its 
global adaptability to item pairs, leading to suboptimal performance. To address 
this issue, we introduce a novel approach, called Probabilistic Metric Learning 
with Adaptive Margin (PMLAM), which dynamically adjusts the margin for each 
pair. By incorporating a probabilistic model, our method ensures that the 
recommended item distance is lower than its alternative. Moreover, the 
probabilistic model enables the integration of a margin term that is 
complementary to the traditional distance contrastive term, thus enhancing the 
model's robustness. Our experimental results on two real-world datasets 
demonstrate the efficacy of our method in achieving superior performance over 
state-of-the-art techniques.

A unital quantum channel's non-Markovianity can be definitively proven by finding a specific state for which the channel produces a non-trivial, non-positive quantum process matrix. In contrast, for non-unital channels, this verification involves a more complex process. Various criteria have been proposed to identify non-Makovian channels, but these do not provide a definitive proof. In this context, we present a novel, direct criterion to conclusively demonstrate the non-Markovianity of any quantum channel, regardless of its unital or non-unital nature.

In various fields, the cost of labeling data can be prohibitively expensive, especially in specialized domains. Active learning addresses this challenge by allowing the system to selectively request labels on only the most uncertain data points. This paper presents a novel active learning approach, which integrates a classifier with a counterfactual reasoning module. The counterfactual module generates hypothetical data points that could have been chosen by the classifier, and their distribution is used to estimate uncertainty. The classifier's uncertainty is then refined using this information, and the most confident regions are excluded from consideration. The remaining data points are selected for active learning, where their labels are requested and the selection process repeated. Experimental results demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, outperforming current methods across various datasets.

A semantic map provides a detailed understanding of an environment's layout and its various components such as obstacles, openings, and objects. This type of map serves as a crucial framework for developing autonomous robots. To create such maps, robots must be able to detect and classify objects in real-time. This paper introduces a novel dataset, known as the RoSmEEry dataset, designed to evaluate the effectiveness of semantic mapping algorithms. The dataset features a comprehensive environment with various objects, including static elements like tables and chairs, as well as dynamic objects like robots in motion. RoSmEEry dataset is designed to simulate real-world scenarios, including objects moving in different directions and objects that are partially hidden from view. This dataset is available for public use, and it is expected to facilitate research in the field of semantic mapping.

Rikudo is a simplified version of Sudoku that retains its complexity. The game is played by filling in numbers on a 9x9 grid, with 3 rows, 2 columns, and 1 square already filled in by the opponent. The objective is to find and mark all empty spaces that could be filled with a single number. The game's validity is determined by ensuring each row, column, and square follows the standard rules, with the twist that certain cells are already revealed. Interestingly, this task has been proven to be computationally challenging, with a high level of complexity that makes it difficult to find efficient solutions.

Optimal transport's computational analysis has a long history, dating back to the 1960s, but the past decade has seen a surge in research on algorithms for approximating transport plans, driven in part by the increased availability of efficient and scalable solutions to the associated optimal transport problem. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of optimal transport computation, highlighting key advancements and areas for further development.

This study delves into the connection between Hecke groups and Ramanujan's modular equations. Specifically, we establish that each modular equation related to Hecke's group Gamma_1(6n) can be expressed as a linear combination of the Eisenstein series, which corresponds to the level 6n. Additionally, we provide a formula to calculate the coefficients of these linear combinations and provide examples for various values of n.

We have obtained high-resolution Keck ESI spectra of six lensed quasars and two multiple-imaged quasar systems, allowing us to determine the redshifts and velocity dispersions of the intervening lensing galaxies. Our analysis of the lensing galaxies' spectra reveals that five are elliptical galaxies, one is a spiral galaxy, and two are likely to be spiral galaxies. We have calculated the redshifts of the lensing galaxies, as well as their velocity dispersions, which range from 150 to 350 km/s. Our results also indicate that the velocity dispersion of the lensing galaxy in the case of HE 0435-1223 is significantly lower than previously thought, a discrepancy that could be resolved by a more accurate measurement of the galaxy's image positions.

This study introduces a discrete model for solving nonlinear q-fractional differential equations on a time scale. We analyze the local uniqueness and global existence of the proposed scheme. Our findings demonstrate that the discrete solution approaches the corresponding q-fractional solution of the differential equation as the time scale's grain size tends to zero. Notably, the discrete solution is more efficient and cost-effective compared to its continuous counterpart. To validate our results, we conduct numerical experiments on several test cases.

The significance of phonons in magnetic materials stems from their role in ferroelectricity and antiferromagnetism, as well as their impact on the topological properties of magnetic insulators. In this study, we investigate the phonon properties of the quantum antiferromagnet Ba$_2$CoRuO$_6$, specifically its magnetic field-induced phase transitions. Through a combination of neutron scattering and density functional theory calculations, we identified two phonon modes that exhibit non-trivial behavior in response to a magnetic field. These modes undergo topological transitions at critical magnetic field thresholds, and their behavior is influenced by the phonon's symmetry and the magnetic field orientation. Our findings demonstrate the phonon Hall effect's occurrence in Ba$_2$CoRuO$_6$ and provide new insights into the topological properties of phonons in magnetic insulators.

A novel, wide-field imaging approach, known as WFSIRDs, utilizes a modified version of Raman shift imaging technology. This technique employs a nod-and-shuffle strategy, where a camera captures two images at separate wavelengths, and a Raman shift module induces a third image at an intermediate wavelength, generating a Raman shift difference spectrum for each pixel. WFSIRDs is a highly efficient method for acquiring Raman spectra, as it requires no camera motion and a single exposure to generate a spectrum for each point in a scene. This technique was successfully demonstrated using a 10 nm Raman shift step, and it was used to generate Raman spectra for a wide field of view scene by scanning the scene under a fixed Raman excitation laser beam. This technique was applied to image a 1mm^2 area of a tobacco leaf, and it was used to identify the spatial distribution of nicotine within the leaf.

This research introduces matrix versions of Fej\'{e}r and Levin-Ste\v{c}kin inequalities for Hermitian matrices. Additionally, the study establishes connections between these inequalities on Hermitian matrices to well-known classical inequalities, including those by Kantorovich and Markov. Furthermore, the concept of a Hermitian operator is expanded to matrix Fej\'{e}r and Levin-Ste\v{c}kin inequalities.

We investigate the average energy condition for a black hole that loses mass over time. The condition is met if the integrated mass flux from infinity to a specific point, where the horizon is located, always has the same sign as the horizon's mass. The integrated mass flux from infinity to the horizon's end point is always non-negative, regardless of the point considered. The condition is met if the horizon's mass loss rate is constant. We also find that near the point where the horizon ends, the mass loss rate varies in proportion to the inverse square of the distance from that point.

This thesis delves into the intricate structure of Conformal Field Theory (CFT) and explores its core principles. Firstly, it delves into the underlying geometry of 2D CFT and examines the properties of CFT on a torus through a series of precise calculations. Next, it introduces a novel approach to defining the partition function of 3D CFT on a line using a mathematical framework based on the Polyakov action. Furthermore, it investigates the concept of entanglement entropy within the context of CFT, applying a rigorous method to derive entropy from the torus partition function. Additionally, it investigates the properties of CFT in the presence of gravity, specifically through a detailed examination of the holographic entropy of entanglement in the AdS$_3$ scenario. Ultimately, this thesis also explores the concept of conformal blocks in CFT, providing a precise mathematical formulation and examining its properties.

The rapid expansion of Industrial Control Systems' capabilities through Industrial Internet of Things technologies has led to increased exposure of critical infrastructure to cyber threats. As a result, there is a pressing need for improved cybersecurity measures. The development of the ICS-CTM model has facilitated the implementation of cybersecurity best practices by providing a structured approach for organizations to evaluate, improve, and integrate cybersecurity methods. Building upon the ICS-CTM model, this research introduces the ICS-CTM2 framework, which addresses the need for practical applications of ICS-CTM. The ICS-CTM2 model is designed to facilitate the implementation of cybersecurity testbeds within organizations, enabling the development of tailored solutions for specific use cases. The ICS-CTM2 framework provides a structured approach for organizations to evaluate, improve, and integrate cybersecurity methods, facilitating the development of practical solutions for real-world challenges.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, the complexity of the state space grows exponentially with the number of agents, making it difficult to develop effective learning methods. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new approach that focuses on a subset of agents at a time, using a greedy-based method to select agents and update joint action values. This approach enables the incorporation of existing single-agent algorithms and their extension to multi-agent systems. The proposed method is capable of generating a compact representation of overall value by aggregating the rewards of a subset of agents. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in a decentralized setting and show that it outperforms a baseline approach, while also achieving a higher degree of parallelization.

Pretrained language models have been found to hold and perpetuate stereotypical biases, yet the impact of these biases on downstream task performance remains poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we introduce StereoSet, a benchmarking dataset designed to assess the extent of stereotypical biases in pre-trained language models. StereoSet comprises 1,500 pairs of sentences that convey the same meaning with varying social attributes (e.g., gender, age, or race) and is annotated according to the LIP framework to classify 11 different bias types. We evaluate the effectiveness of fine-tuning StereoSet on 11 tasks, including sentiment analysis and negation detection, and discover that stereotypical biases are consistently transferred to the downstream tasks, influencing the models' performance. Notably, we observe that biases are particularly pronounced in specific subgroups, such as individuals with non-traditional gender identities, and that biases related to social class tend to be the most prevalent. StereoSet is publicly available and can be accessed at https://github.com/allenai/stereoset.

In wireless communication systems, Remote Electrical Tilt (RET) plays a crucial role in optimizing Base Station (BS) coverage and capacity by adjusting the beam pattern. However, the optimal RET values are difficult to determine due to the complex interactions between signal propagation, hardware limitations, and user behavior. To address this challenge, we present an off-policy reinforcement learning method to find the optimal RET settings that maximize user throughput and minimize energy consumption. Our approach uses a neural network to approximate the optimal policy, which is trained on a dataset collected from a remote antenna system. The learning algorithm can adapt to changing user behavior and hardware dynamics without requiring a model of the environment. Experimental results show that our method outperforms traditional approaches by 10-20% in maximizing user throughput and reducing energy consumption.

A multi-measurement approach has been implemented to determine the CKM angle gamma, leveraging the individual results from the LHCb experiment. The analysis incorporates two types of decays: B+ to D+ tau minus tau plus and B- to D0 (bar) tau minus tau plus decays, which have been analyzed in earlier studies. The present investigation involves combining the results from these decays, utilizing additional data from the LHCb experiment, resulting in a world-best determination of gamma, with a value at 57 degrees and a one-standard-deviation interval of 46 to 68 degrees.

We investigate the properties of complex ellipsoids, specifically the condition for the reverse arithmetic mean inequality in the context of n-dimensional complex space. Alongside the relevant criteria for convex bodies, we also examine the characteristics of complex ellipsoids in relation to their real counterparts and dimensions of lower or higher dimensions.

The collection, dissemination, and commercial exploitation of personal data pose significant privacy concerns. The potential risks and benefits of data markets remain a topic of debate among researchers and policymakers. To gain insight into public perceptions of data markets, we conducted a study involving 160 participants, surveying them on their willingness to monetize their personal data. The results indicate that the majority of participants are unwilling to sell data for financial gain, but a substantial percentage would consider it if they could control how it's used, and privacy protection laws existed. Additionally, participants' motivations for data-selling varied, with a significant proportion wanting to use the funds for personal benefits. The study also found that individuals' privacy concerns differ from their willingness to monetize data, and participants' attitudes towards data markets were influenced by their subjective moral attitudes.

In faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling, the receiver faces significant challenges when trying to recover the original symbols, particularly when using non-uniform sampling rates. This research focuses on the development of a universal detection system for FTN signaling that can handle any sampling rate increase. A novel deep learning-based approach to list sphere decoding (LSD) is proposed, which involves training a neural network to map the received samples to the corresponding constellation points. This method is particularly effective for moderate signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) and is further enhanced by incorporating a specialized unit to handle real-valued constellation symbols. The results show that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms traditional methods, achieving a 2.5 dB improvement in bit error rate (BER) for QPSK-modulated FTN signaling with a 1.5-fold increase in sampling rate.

We focus on two topological structures, the Frink ideal topology and order topology, within an effect algebra, considering their properties and relationships, as well cross-referencing connections to the Riesz decomposition property. We establish that in finite effect algebras possessing a certain Riesz decomposition property, Frink ideal topology converges to order topology. We further explore the concept of continuity in both topological structures, as well as their interaction with the Riesz decomposition property. We demonstrate that every non-trivial finite Boolean algebra exhibits the Riesz decomposition property under both topological structures, while also showing that 4-element algebra has continuous order topology but discontinuous Frink ideal topology. We establish that Riesz decomposition property is preserved under continuous functions within both topological structures, while also proving that every non-separable, infinite Boolean algebra has discontinuous order topology but continuous Frink ideal topology. We establish that 4-element algebra is homeomorphic to both its Frink ideal and order topologies, while also proving that 8-element algebra has homeomorphic Frink ideal and order topologies. We further explore the concept of continuity in both topologies, as well as their interaction with the Riesz decomposition property. We also provide examples of non-continuous topological structures within both.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of highly accurate models, but these models often rely on overfitting to the training data and demonstrate poor generalization. To mitigate this issue, data augmentation techniques have been employed to enhance model generalization, but the current methods lack a clear understanding of the target data distribution. To address this limitation, this study introduces SaliencyMix, a novel data augmentation strategy that leverages saliency maps to identify the most critical features of the target data distribution.
